evidence: Rust/run.sh lines 38-43: 'if [ $? -eq 0 ]' after 'cargo build --release' — with set -e active, this branch is unreachable on failure; the build failure path at line 75-78 can never execute
Rust/run.sh lines 43-73: nested 'if [ $? -eq 0 ]' inside the outer success branch after 'cargo run --release' — same issue, set -e makes the else branch dead code
Cpp/run.sh lines 40-43: same set -e + explicit $? check pattern — 'if [ $? -eq 0 ]' after 'make' is always-true under set -e; the else branch at lines 60-62 is dead
Scala/run.sh lines 29-35 and 45-51: 'if [ $? -eq 0 ]' after sbt/scalac invocations with set -e active — both else branches are unreachable dead code

status_dashboard.sh line 60: 'if ls $main_file 1> /dev/null 2>&1' — the $main_file variable is unquoted, which means glob expansion happens before ls, so the condition behaves differently than a naive reader would expect (it tests whether at least one file matching the glob exists, not whether the literal path exists)

Shell/Active_Shellference.sh calculate_vfe(): the function body is solely 'vfe=$(calculate_kl_divergence beliefs_ref preferences_ref); echo "$vfe"' — an always-true pass-through with no additional logic

run_all.sh lines 253-255: 'if [ $SUCCESS_COUNT -eq $TOTAL_IMPLEMENTATIONS ]' checks whether ALL implementations succeeded, but FAILURE_COUNT is printed conditionally on line 247 only when > 0; a partial success with FAILURE_COUNT=0 is impossible (SUCCESS+FAILURE always equals TOTAL when all loops complete), so the final success message triggers correctly but the logic is not self-evident

strengths: run_all.sh's parallel execution path correctly tracks PIDs and waits on each before incrementing counters — the logic is sound even if the encoding is verbose
Shell/config.sh validate_config() uses bc -l comparisons consistently and returns a clear non-zero exit code on any validation failure
Most run.sh scripts use guard clauses at the top (command -v checks) before doing any work, which is intention-revealing and avoids deep nesting
logic_clarity.issue_character: The dominant issue is the pervasive dead-code pattern: multiple run.sh scripts use 'set -e' at the top and then add 'if [ $? -eq 0 ]' branches after commands, making the failure branches unreachable — this is a codebase-wide copy-paste pattern rather than isolated incidents.
logic_clarity.score_rationale: The guard-clause pattern at the tops of scripts and the validation logic in config.sh are genuinely clear. However, the dead-code pattern (set -e + $? checks) appears in at least four language runners (Rust, C++, Scala) and potentially more, meaning a developer reading those files will encounter branches that look like they handle failures but will never execute. The calculate_vfe pass-through adds another logic-clarity concern. These are not isolated rough edges — they are a systemic pattern across the codebase. This places the score in the 65–70 range: 'mixed', where a developer cannot fully trust the control flow they read.

issues.summary: Rust/run.sh uses set -e but tests $? after cargo build and cargo run — failure else-branches are dead code
evidence: Line 5: set -e causes the script to exit immediately on any non-zero exit
Lines 36-79: 'if [ $? -eq 0 ]' wraps cargo build output; the else branch at line 75 ('echo "❌ Rust build failed."') can never execute because set -e would have already exited
Same pattern repeated for cargo run on lines 43-74
issues.suggestion: Remove the $? checks and rely on set -e for failure detection, or remove 'set -e' and use explicit error handling. The simplest fix: remove the outer if/else wrappers and let set -e propagate failures naturally.

issues.summary: Cpp/run.sh uses set -e but tests $? after make and ./ActiveInferenceDemo — failure else-branches are dead code
evidence: Lines 40-62: nested if [ $? -eq 0 ] after make; the else at line 60 ('echo "❌ C++ build failed."') is unreachable under set -e
issues.suggestion: Remove the $? conditional wrappers and let set -e handle failures, matching the simpler pattern used in Ada/run.sh, Elixir/run.sh, and Erlang/run.sh.

issues.summary: Scala/run.sh uses set -e but tests $? after sbt and scalac invocations — failure else-branches are dead code
evidence: Lines 29-35: if [ $? -eq 0 ] after sbt run; else branch ('echo "❌ SBT execution failed."') is unreachable
Lines 45-51: same pattern for the scala fallback path
issues.suggestion: Remove $? checks and rely on set -e, matching the simpler pattern used in Elixir/run.sh and Erlang/run.sh.

issues.summary: calculate_vfe() is a trivial pass-through to calculate_kl_divergence() with no added logic, making it a dead abstraction that obscures the identity of the two computations
evidence: Lines 70-77: calculate_vfe() calls calculate_kl_divergence() and echoes the result unchanged — the functions are logically identical in this implementation
run_simulation() calls both calculate_vfe and calculate_kl_divergence indirectly, creating a confusing dual-name for the same operation
issues.suggestion: Either implement actual VFE logic that extends beyond KL divergence (e.g. add a likelihood term), or inline the KL divergence call in run_simulation() and remove calculate_vfe(), adding a comment explaining why VFE equals KL divergence in this simplified model.

root_causes: The run.sh scripts appear to have been generated from a template that included set -e for safety but also included explicit $? checks for error messages — combining both is a well-known shell anti-pattern that results in dead else-branches across all scripts that used the template
